lesson_title: Taps and Drains: the Four-Sector Circular Flow
hook_text: The whole economy is a water tank on a stand — three taps, three drains, one level.
clip_script: Picture the town's big water tank. Taps above, drains below, and the LEVEL of the water is the size of the economy — national income. Three drains carry money out. Part of every salary gets SAVED: it rests in the bank instead of reaching a till. Part gets TAXED: the payslip arrives lighter than the salary. Part buys IMPORTS: that money sails away in a container. Save, tax, import. Three taps pour money in. A business borrows and instals new sewing lines — investment. Government spends on the clinic, the teachers, the road. And foreign shops pay for the town's jeans — exports. Now the only rule that matters: the level holds when the taps TOGETHER match the drains TOGETHER. Not tap for drain. Together. So what is a recession? A tap chokes. Europe cuts its orders — jeans stack up in the storeroom, the factory drops a shift, payslips thin, the corner shop trims its own orders, around and around. And here is the part nobody tells you: the level DOES settle again — lower. Poorer people save less, pay less tax, import less, so the drains narrow until it all balances. Balanced — with a shift's worth of workers at home. Balanced is not the same as well.
visual_style: A raised water tank drawn over a factory-town street: taps labelled as sewing lines, a clinic and a container ship; drains labelled as a bank, a payslip and a departing container; the waterline dropping and settling as a shift light switches off.
mood: Calm and clear, tightening into hard truth.
pacing: Unhurried through the three drains and three taps, then quickening turn by turn as the level falls, ending on a still line.
